sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Can a first-time viewer say in one sentence what this piece is for?** and **Does each heading name what its section holds?** No to both. The page title "Rainfall at the reservoir" (120–480, 55–90) promises one subject. The page then shows an unlabelled chart (120–640, 136–495) next to a "Getting there" column (640–1000, 140–280) about the bus, parking and cycle racks, which has nothing to do with rainfall. A first-time viewer can't decide whether this is a rainfall report or a visitor info page, and the title describes only half of what the page holds. Defect (a page with two competing messages is common sense here; the catalog's source for this line is off the approved list). WCAG 2.4.6 asks headings to describe their content, and the page title doesn't cover the directions. Direction: choose what the page is for. If it's a visitor page, retitle it for the place and make rainfall one labelled section. If it's a rainfall report, move the directions somewhere else. Weight: major.
2. **Do the main image and the headline make one idea together, with neither just repeating the other?** No. The chart is the main image, but it has no values, units, time period or category labels, so all it adds to the headline is "some bars, one taller." Together they say "rainfall exists" and nothing more: no point such as "wettest month was March" or "rain is down this year." Defect: the viewer gets the topic but no information. This is judged as common sense, since the catalog's source is off the list. Direction: give the pair one claim. Have the headline state the finding and label the chart so it proves it. (Labelling details belong to the data section.) Weight: major.
3. **Does every element, rule, box, and ornament do a job, so that removing it would lose something?** No. The chart sits inside a thick dark-grey frame, about 3 px (120–640, 136–495), with a pale blue fill. The frame is the darkest, heaviest line on the page after the title. It competes with the bars and walls the chart off from the text beside it, and it carries no information. Convention (Tufte, *The Visual Display of Quantitative Information*, ch. 4–5, non-data ink. Lupton, *Thinking with Type*, "Data tables": replace rules with space or a pale tone). Direction: remove the border and keep the pale tone, or just use space. Weight: minor.

**What's working.** The type, the single blue and the flat shapes all share one plain, neutral voice. Nothing looks pasted in from another style, so once the content question is settled the piece will hold together visually.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 4 yes, 4 no (one-sentence purpose; image and headline make one idea; every element does a job; headings name their sections), 0 unsure

**Section.** What matters first: applies. The page has a title, a chart and a block of text with its own heading. I could not run the crop and entries scripts because Bash was denied, so I judged from the full 1280×800 image alone.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The page has a clear order.** The chart panel (about x 120–640, y 136–495) is the largest and strongest thing on the page: a tinted, bordered box with three saturated blue bars. It clearly leads, so the eye knows where to start. The bold title "Rainfall at the reservoir" at the top left (about 32 px) holds its place above it because it is very dark and comes first, so you read title → chart → side text without hesitation. Keep the chart as the one heavy mass. Don't let the side column grow to match it.
- **The text has three clear levels:** title (about 32 px bold), the heading "Getting there" (about 20 px bold) and body (about 17 px regular). The heading is both bigger and bolder than the body, so it reads as a heading at a glance even though the sizes are only a few pixels apart. The jump from title to heading is large, so the two never get confused.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** I estimated the type sizes by eye. If the director wants to check that the heading and body are far enough apart, the exact sizes need measuring, since a measured facts file was not provided.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **The "Getting there" text is stuck to the chart.** This covers four checklist lines: *Do all blocks… take their edges and the gaps between them from one grid…?*, *Is the space inside each group clearly smaller than the space between groups…?*, *Do only related elements look alike, with no accidental groups…?* and *Does each element stay clear of the others, with no text or box overlapping or touching another?*
   - **Where:** the chart panel's right border ends at about x=639. The "Getting there" heading and paragraph start at about x=641, so there is no gutter.
   - **What the viewer sees:** the gap between the chart and the text (about 0 px) is smaller than the gap inside the text group (about 10 px from heading to body). Closeness is the strongest grouping cue, so bus times and parking read as the chart's caption or legend. A reader looking for what the bars mean will look there first and find directions instead. The title "Rainfall at the reservoir" sits over both blocks, which makes the false link stronger.
   - **Why:** Arnheim and Wertheimer on grouping by closeness (*Unrelated elements do not crowd each other*, *Space shows the groups*). Müller-Brockmann asks for a fixed gap between grid fields (*Equal intervals between columns*). The touching itself is common sense.
   - **Fix:** put the two blocks on a column grid with a real gutter, wider than any gap inside a group (at least as big as the 48 px gap under the title). Better still, separate the topics clearly: give the directions their own section with space above it, below the chart or in a clearly separate column, so it can't be read as part of the chart.
   - **Type:** defect. **Weight:** major.
2. ***Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?***
   - **Where:** all the content is in the top-left area, roughly x 120–1000 and y 50–495. The heaviest thing on the page, the dark-bordered chart with saturated blue bars, sits at the far left. The right margin (about 280 px) is more than twice the left margin (120 px), and the bottom 300 px are empty.
   - **What the viewer sees:** the page looks pushed up and to the left. It reads as content that hasn't filled its layout, or a page that didn't finish loading, not as a planned asymmetric composition.
   - **Why:** Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance": a heavy side needs a counterweight.
   - **Fix:** either give the composition a counterweight (widen the text column, or let the chart span the content width with the text below it), or centre the content block in the viewport so the empty space reads as margin.
   - **Type:** defect. **Weight:** minor. The page still works, but it looks unfinished.
3. ***Do the main divisions of the frame follow one proportion…?***
   - **Where:** the horizontal splits are about 120 (margin), 520 (chart), 360 (text) and 280 (margin). They share no ratio, and the chart's 360 px height doesn't relate to the text block either.
   - **What the viewer sees:** the widths look like whatever the parts happened to be, not a planned division of the frame.
   - **Fix:** take the widths from one column count, for example a 12-column grid with the chart at 7 columns, the text at 5, and equal outer margins.
   - **Type:** taste. **Weight:** minor.

**What's working.**
- The title and the chart's left edge share the line at x=120, so the page's one strong vertical holds.
- Inside the text block, the heading sits close to its paragraph (about 10 px) with comfortable line spacing, so that small group reads as one unit.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 7 yes, 6 no (one grid; space within groups smaller than between; no accidental groups; elements clear of each other; balance; one proportion), 0 unsure.

I checked only the Charts and data part of the checklist. The chart has nothing on it saying what the bars measure, so as it stands it tells the viewer nothing.

**Section.** Charts and data: applies. There is one bar chart with three bars in a single series.

**Findings**
1. **"Does each chart name what its marks show, with axis values, units, and series labels?"** No.
   - **Where:** The chart (x 120–640, y 136–495) has three blue bars (x ≈183–271, 311–399, 439–527) on a grey baseline at y ≈ 453. It has no category labels under the bars, no y axis, no tick values, no value labels on the bars and no unit.
   - **What the viewer meets:** They can see that the middle bar is about 1.5 times the left one and about twice the right one. They cannot tell which periods or places the bars are, or how much rain any bar is. The title says "rainfall", so the viewer reasonably expects amounts (mm, by month or year) and gets only proportions. The chart fails the one job it has.
   - **Why:** Tufte, *The Visual Display of Quantitative Information*, ch. 2, and Few, *Show Me the Numbers*: the reader should never have to guess what a number measures.
   - **Two other lines fail for the same reason, so they belong to this finding:**
     - "Does each chart show enough of the time range or sample to judge the trend?" No. With three unnamed bars, nobody can tell whether three periods are enough context or a chosen slice (common sense).
     - "Are categorical bars sorted by value or by a natural order?" No. The bars run medium, high, low. That is only fine if they follow a natural order such as time, and nothing on the chart shows that (Few; Wilke, *Fundamentals of Data Visualization*).
   - **Fix:** Put a category label under each bar, such as the month or year, and a value with its unit on or above each bar (e.g. "84 mm"). With direct values you don't need a y axis. If the categories are periods, keep them in time order and label them so the order reads as time.
   - **Kind and weight:** Defect, major.

2. **"Does a title or caption state the chart's finding in words?"** No.
   - **Where:** The heading "Rainfall at the reservoir" (x 120–480, y ≈ 55–90).
   - **What the viewer meets:** The heading names a topic, not a finding. Even after labels are added, the viewer has to work out the point alone, e.g. whether the last period was a dry one.
   - **Why:** The catalog's sources for this rule are not on the approved list, so this is taste and common sense. A title that says what the data shows tells the casual visitor why the chart is there.
   - **Fix:** Add a title or one-line caption that states the takeaway, e.g. "[Month] was the wettest of the three; rainfall then fell by half." The section heading can stay above it.
   - **Kind and weight:** Taste, minor. It only matters once finding 1 is fixed.

3. **"Is nearly all the ink in each chart data, with no 3D, shadows, textures, or heavy gridlines?"** No.
   - **Where:** A dark slate frame about 3 px thick and a pale blue-grey panel fill surround the whole chart (x 120–640, y 136–495).
   - **What the viewer meets:** The frame is the darkest line on the chart after the bars. It reads as the edge of a box, not as part of the data. It also runs right up to the "Getting there" text, so the chart looks like a widget rather than a figure.
   - **Why:** Wilke, *Fundamentals of Data Visualization*, ch. 23.2, and Tufte, ch. 5: the data marks should be the darkest lines in the chart.
   - **Fix:** Remove the frame, or make it a thin pale grey line, and drop or lighten the fill so the bars and baseline carry the chart.
   - **Kind and weight:** Convention, minor.

**What's working.**
- **One colour and flat bars.** The single strong blue on plain bars has no 3D, gradients or gridlines. That suits a single series and should stay when labels are added.
- **Bar spacing.** The bars are evenly spaced, with gaps a little under their width, so they compare cleanly.

**Checklist.** Charts and data: 16 lines, 11 yes, 5 no (marks named with axis values, units and labels; enough time range; bars sorted; title states the finding; ink mostly data)

**Section.** Interface: skipped. There are no controls on this page: no buttons, links, fields, menus or navigation. It has a title, a framed bar chart and a "Getting there" text block.

**Findings**
None.

**Checklist.** Interface: skipped
